operationalization: Code each species as air-breathing or gill-breathing and as internally viviparous (live birth with the embryo retained and nourished in the mother, rather than an egg laid to the outside). The claim is refuted by viviparous gill-breathers and supported if internal viviparity is confined to air-breathers in the compiled tables.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and respiration for bony and cartilaginous fishes, including viviparous species

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: elasmobranch reproductive mode, including placental and other forms of live birth

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian viviparity and gestation as the air-breathing comparison class

obstacles: Aristotle's 'internally viviparous' has to be separated from egg-laying and from yolk-only retention.
FishBase sometimes lumps ovoviviparity with viviparity.
rationale: Live birth and mode of respiration are standard fields for fishes and mammals. Open compilations cover the gill-breathing groups in which exceptions would appear, and a single well-coded viviparous shark or teleost decides the universal claim. The remaining work is a coding crosswalk, which is routine.

operationalization: Compare adult body temperature or mass-specific metabolic rate of lunged versus lungless species, and among lunged species compare richly vascularized lungs with simpler ones. Higher values in lunged animals, and the highest in soft blood-rich lungs, would support the claim; a reversal in a broad sample would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: species-level body temperature and metabolic rate, concentrated on birds and mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: metabolic and life-history parameters across animals, including many ectotherms

obstacles: Aristotle's heat is an innate quality only partly captured by body temperature or metabolic rate.
Endothermy, body size and environment are confounded with presence of a lung.
rationale: Temperature and metabolic-rate tables exist and can rank many lunged and lungless species. Coverage is thin for fishes and amphibians relative to birds and mammals, and a temperature ranking does not isolate the lung from endothermy. The test is informative for a physiological proxy on a subset of taxa.

operationalization: Assign independent proxies of heat (body temperature or metabolic rate) and of dryness (cutaneous water loss or egg water content) and test whether those proxies predict cleidoic eggs in birds and scaly reptiles versus live birth. The heat-and-moisture rule fails if reproductive mode does not track the proxies once phylogeny is taken into account.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: parity mode, clutch size and related life-history traits for birds, mammals and reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: body temperature for endotherms as a proxy for Aristotle's heat

obstacles: Dryness and innate heat are largely read off the reproductive modes they are meant to explain.
Viviparity in reptiles tracks climate and phylogeny at least as closely as any moisture score.
rationale: Parity mode is tabulated for amniotes, so the pattern of complete eggs versus live birth can be plotted. Independent measurements of dryness are scattered, and heat is a poor separator once birds, mammals and reptiles are compared. Outcomes remain compatible with several causal stories, so only a proxy of the mechanism can be tested.

operationalization: Map 'scolex' to a larval stage unlike the adult, then score insects for presence of a larva and for red blood or hemoglobin, and score non-insects for larvae. Any ametabolous insect, any blooded larva-producer, or an insect with hemoglobin-bearing blood challenges the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: documented holometabolous life cycle and developmental stages for Drosophila

candidate_datasets.name: AmphiBIO
candidate_datasets.role: amphibian reproductive modes, including larval stages in blooded animals

obstacles: Aristotle's scolex is a grub that later hardens, not every modern larval type.
Insect life-history traits are not in one global downloadable matrix.
rationale: Model-organism and amphibian trait tables can test pieces of the conjunction: fly metamorphosis, and blooded animals with larvae. A full survey of insect orders, and of which insects lack hemoglobin, still has to be compiled from the literature. The universal quantifiers are decidable on a subset, which is why the claim is only partly resolvable.

operationalization: No measurement separates a 'right' ranking by perfection and innate heat from the bare list of reproductive modes, because perfection and heat are assigned from those same modes.
obstacles: 'More perfect' and 'hotter' are not defined independently of the reproductive series.
A teleological claim that nature orders generation rightly has no rival-excluding observation.
rationale: Reproductive modes can be listed, and life-history databases already list them, but the claim is that nature grades animals by perfection and heat. Those ranks are not additional observations. Any outcome of a mode table can be read as fitting the scale, so the claim is not empirically decidable.

operationalization: Using staged embryo series, record whether distinct organs are present together at the earliest stage or appear across successive stages. Simultaneous presence of the later organs at the first morphological stage would refute successive formation; a repeated sequence of appearance would confirm it.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish staging series showing organs appearing across developmental stages

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Xenopus developmental stages and organogenesis images

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick gene-expression and anatomical stages through organogenesis

obstacles: Public staging atlases cover model species rather than every animal phylum.
rationale: Successive versus simultaneous appearance of parts is directly visible in open staging series for fishes, amphibians and birds, and the same contrast can be checked in insect resources. That is enough to confirm or refute the general embryological claim with standard inspection of existing images and stage tables. Remaining taxa would widen coverage rather than change the decision criterion.

operationalization: In lunged vertebrates, record the stage of first morphological appearance of the heart and of the lung bud, and their relative sizes at those stages. Heart-before-lung despite a larger lung confirms the claim; lung-before-heart, or a lung that is smaller when it first appears, refutes the stated contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick stages covering early heart and later respiratory-tract markers

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: frog organogenesis, with heart formation preceding lung development

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: timed mouse developmental series for early organ landmarks, strongest for the head and neural tube

obstacles: A quantitative heart-versus-lung size table is not precompiled across species.
The mouse atlas is brain-centered, so lung timing leans on chick and frog resources plus the literature.
rationale: The order of appearance and the relative size of heart and lung are observable in existing vertebrate staging series, especially chick and frog. Those series cover a subset of lunged animals rather than the full scope. The comparison itself is unambiguous once the stages are aligned, so the restricted taxonomic window is the main limit.

operationalization: Measure semen colour, viscosity and freezing behaviour at emission and after cooling, including near-freezing temperatures. Thick white semen that becomes colourless and watery on cooling, and that fails to freeze in frost, would support the claim; stable colour or ordinary freezing would refute the corresponding clause.
obstacles: Quantitative cooling curves are scattered in andrology and animal-breeding papers rather than one open table.
Most measurements are human or livestock, not animals generally.
rationale: Colour, viscosity and whether semen freezes are laboratory variables with a clear decision rule. Published descriptions and cryopreservation reports cover humans and a few domestic species, and they have to be compiled. A systematic multi-species cooling series is not a single public dataset, so only part of the scope can be checked now.

operationalization: Record ejaculate colour across human populations, including dark-skinned African populations, and across other animals. Universally white or grey semen supports the claim; a population whose semen is black refutes it.
obstacles: No open dataset stratifies semen colour by ancestry.
Clinical series are scattered and rarely designed as a population survey.
rationale: Semen colour is directly observable, and the Herodotus clause names a specific human contrast. Andrology reports describe colour repeatedly, but they are papers rather than a downloadable multi-population table. A small team can compile the human evidence; a true global sample of animals is thinner.

operationalization: Order embryonic characters by stage of first appearance and class them as shared among animals or peculiar to a species. Species-specific characters appearing after the shared ones would support the claim; early appearance of species-specific traits, under a pre-registered character list, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish stage tables for the order in which structures appear

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick expression and anatomy through stages where species characters differentiate

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: frog developmental stages for comparing shared and later characters

obstacles: Which characters count as 'generic animal' versus species-specific is contested.
Transcriptomic hourglass tests are a rival operationalization with different datasets.
rationale: Staging atlases contain the raw sequence of morphological appearance for several vertebrates. Turning that sequence into a test requires a character partition that is not in the atlases themselves. Competing partitions change the result, so the claim is testable only after a substantial coding choice and only for well-staged species.

operationalization: No observation distinguishes reason entering the embryo from outside, and being divine, from the fact that humans reason, because 'from outside' and 'divine' name no measurable variable.
obstacles: The claim is a doctrine about soul, not a prediction about organs or timing.
A strong reading that equates reason with absence of brain activity changes what Aristotle meant.
rationale: The sentence asserts an external, divine origin for reason and denies a bodily activity proper to it in his psychological sense. That is not a staging, anatomical or physiological measurement. Brain-activity datasets would test a different claim about neural correlates, not this one.

operationalization: Code chondrichthyan species for whether embryos finish development by a maternal uterine connection after yolk stores are used, and whether the egg is laid. One or more species with retained, maternally attached embryos confirms the existential claim; none in a broad elasmobranch sample would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode of sharks and rays, including placental viviparity

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species-level reproductive mode for cartilaginous fishes

obstacles: 'Connection with the uterus' covers several matrotrophic modes that databases code under broader labels.
rationale: The claim is existential: some selachians keep the embryo and nourish it from the mother. Reproductive-mode fields already separate egg-laying, yolk-sac viviparity and placental attachment for many sharks and rays. A standard query of those tables can confirm or refute the existence claim without new collecting.

operationalization: Compare dates of menstrual onset with lunar phase in a large sample of cycles, and separately test whether ambient temperature is lower during the waning moon in the same records. A significant excess of onsets in the waning half would support the timing clause; a flat distribution would refute it.
obstacles: Cycle-onset dates tied to lunar phase sit in scattered studies, not one public table.
The waning moon is a weak stand-in for a colder environment, so the causal clause is confounded.
rationale: Onset versus lunar phase is a clear statistical contrast, and several published cycle series speak to it. Those series are not gathered in an open repository with broad geographic coverage. Temperature as the stated cause is a further claim that lunar phase does not measure, so only the timing clause is partly testable.

operationalization: In multi-generation hybrid pedigrees of the named crosses, score offspring shape against the two parental species and test whether later generations converge on the female parent's form. Convergence on the female line would support the claim; stable intermediacy, male-line resemblance, or sterility that stops the pedigree would refute it for that cross.
obstacles: Fox-dog and partridge-fowl crosses rarely yield the successive fertile generations the claim requires.
Hybrid pedigrees with scored morphology are scattered and often unpublished as data tables.
rationale: The prediction is a directional change in resemblance across generations and is measurable where pedigrees exist. The crosses Aristotle names are poorly represented by public multi-generation datasets. Better-documented hybrid zones, such as some canids, can serve only as a proxy and do not cover his examples.

operationalization: In staged vertebrate embryos, rank the heart against other organs by stage of first distinct appearance. The heart earliest in each series supports the claim; any blooded animal in which another organ is distinctly formed before the heart refutes the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish heart development relative to other early structures

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick stages from the heart tube onward

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: frog stages for the timing of heart formation

obstacles: 'First distinctly marked off' depends on what counts as an organ rather than a germ layer.
Model species stand in for all blooded animals.
rationale: Open staging series show when the heart becomes visible in fishes, birds and amphibians. That tests the claim on a real but incomplete sample of vertebrates. Borderline cases, such as notochord or neural tube appearing as early as the heart, keep the test from being fully clean across the whole scope.

operationalization: Once erythrinus is mapped to a modern species or genus, tally sexed specimens and the presence of testes versus ovaries or roe. A substantial sample of functional males refutes the claim; only females, or simultaneous hermaphrodites with no separate male, would support the observation he reports.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: sex, hermaphroditism and reproductive notes for candidate Mediterranean fishes

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic framework for matching ancient fish names to current genera

obstacles: Erythrinus is not a secure identification; serranids and sparids would give different sexual systems.
Hermaphrodites can look like 'females full of roe' without the species lacking males.
rationale: FishBase records sex and hermaphroditism for the plausible modern groups, so the biological test is standard once the name is fixed. The name itself points at more than one Mediterranean fish. Until that mapping is chosen, the same data can both confirm and refute the report.

operationalization: Score Anguilla and candidate stagnant-water mullets for separate males and females using gonad type or genetic sex. Distinct males and females refute 'neither male nor female'; a species with no sex distinction would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: sex, maturity and reproductive biology of eels and mullets

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex
candidate_datasets.role: sexual systems and sex-determination records for fishes

obstacles: The mullet of stagnant waters is not identified to a modern species.
Eel gonads mature at sea, so river samples under-represent sex even though the sexes exist.
rationale: Eel sexual systems are documented in open fish databases well enough to test Aristotle's example directly. The second example, a mullet of stagnant water, cannot be tied to one species with the same confidence. The claim is therefore resolvable for eels and open for the mullet.

operationalization: Among species with separate sexes, record whether females produce viable offspring with no male contribution. Facultative or obligate parthenogenesis in such species refutes the empirical clause; its absence across a broad sample would support it. The maxim that nature makes nothing in vain is not part of the measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex
candidate_datasets.role: sexual systems, including parthenogenesis, across animals

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts for squamates in which facultative parthenogenesis is reported

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive notes for fishes, including rare parthenogenesis

obstacles: 'Perfectly' is undefined: a parthenogenetic offspring may or may not count as complete generation.
The teleological premise is not tested by the reproductive records.
rationale: Sexual-system compilations record parthenogenesis in animals that also have separate sexes, which is the observable part of the claim. Whether an uniparental offspring counts as perfect generation still has to be defined. The maxim that nature makes nothing in vain is not decided by those records.

operationalization: In staged embryos, compare first appearance of internal organs with external structures, and of larger structures with smaller ones. Internal-before-external and large-before-small would support the claim; a repeated external-before-internal sequence would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick stages spanning early external axial structures and internal organs

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish stage series for organ versus body-surface timing

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: frog stages for the order of internal and external structures

obstacles: The boundary between internal and external parts is ambiguous for neural tube, somites and skin.
Visibility depends on staining and on which structures are scored as large.
rationale: Staging series contain the order in which structures become visible for several vertebrates. Applying Aristotle's internal-versus-external cut, and his size rule, requires a coding scheme that the atlases do not supply. The test is feasible for model species and remains sensitive to that coding.

operationalization: For many-toed quadrupeds, record whether eyelids are fused at birth and the age at eye opening. Universal birth with closed eyes in that group would support the claim; a many-toed species born with eyes open would refute the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts stating whether carnivore young are born blind and when the eyes open

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian life-history context, including altricial development where coded

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and neonate traits used to place species as altricial or precocial

obstacles: 'Polydactylous quadrupeds' may mean fissiped carnivores or every many-toed mammal, and those scopes differ.
Age at eye opening is written in species accounts more often than in a single numeric column.
rationale: Eye opening is a standard natural-history fact for the dog, cat and their relatives, and species accounts record it. A downloadable numeric field for every many-toed mammal is lacking, so the universal has to be compiled. Within the named carnivores the test is straightforward; outside that list the category itself is the obstacle.

operationalization: Measure relative volume of head, eyes and legs at early embryonic stages. A head and eyes that dominate early, with small legs, would support the descriptive clause. The claim that lower parts exist for the sake of the upper has no separate measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: timed mouse embryo images for early head and eye proportions

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick embryo images across stages when the head is disproportionately large

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: frog embryo morphology during early body-axis formation

obstacles: The teleological clause is not distinguished from the size pattern it explains.
Public series are model species, and morphometrics would have to be taken from images.
rationale: Early embryos in open atlases can be measured for head, eye and limb proportions, which tests the descriptive half. 'For the sake of the upper parts' adds no further observation. Image measurement is standard but has been done for only some of the animals in scope.

operationalization: Track relative eye size from first appearance to the stage when eyelids, lens and retina are complete, and test for an interval of collapse. Eyes that are disproportionately large early, then collapse, and finish last, would support the claim; eyes that are complete early or that grow steadily without collapse would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GEISHA
candidate_datasets.role: chick eye development from optic vesicle to later ocular structures

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Developing Mouse Brain Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: mouse developmental series covering early optic tissues

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish eye staging from optic vesicle onward

obstacles: 'Collapse' needs a morphometric definition, not just a qualitative impression.
Completion ranks require a full organ checklist that atlases do not precompute.
rationale: Optic-vesicle stages and later eye morphology are documented for chick, mouse and zebrafish. Ranking the eye as the last organ finished, and demonstrating a collapse, needs extra measurement on those images. The pattern can be tested in those model vertebrates and not yet as a finished comparative table.

operationalization: Compare ossification timing of the cranial roof with other skull bones, and fontanelle closure age in humans versus other mammals, alongside relative brain size. A skull roof that ossifies last and stays soft longer in humans would support the descriptive clauses; an earlier-closing human fontanelle, or a later bone elsewhere, would refute them.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: comparative notes on mammalian neonates, skulls and relative brain size

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: life-history context for postnatal development in humans and other mammals

obstacles: Ossification-sequence matrices and fontanelle-closure ages are scattered across papers.
'Most fluid' brain has no standard variable distinct from brain size and water content.
rationale: Fontanelle closure and skull ossification order are measured in human paediatrics and in comparative ossification studies. Those measurements are not one open cross-species file. Relative brain size can be brought in from compilations, while 'most fluid' remains a loose extra clause, so the claim is only partly testable.

operationalization: Compare species with determinate versus continued bone growth on whether body size plateaus when skeletal growth stops. A tight match would support bones as the limit of size; continued body growth after skeletal maturity, or determinate size in animals whose skeleton keeps growing, would weaken that causal claim.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: von Bertalanffy growth parameters showing whether fishes approach an asymptotic length

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian and avian longevity and body size for determinate growers

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: body size and life-history timing across amniotes

obstacles: The counterfactual that bones could always grow is not itself a dataset.
Growth plateaus have hormonal and energetic causes that are confounded with skeletal cessation.
rationale: Asymptotic growth curves and adult body sizes are widely tabulated, so determinate and continued growth can be compared. Those tables do not show that bone is the cause of the plateau. The causal claim stays weakly separated from rival limits on growth.

operationalization: Measure hair shaft length at death and at later intervals on the same body, controlling for skin retraction. Continued elongation of the shaft would support the claim; length change explained by shrinkage of the scalp, with no new hair growth, would refute it.
obstacles: Forensic measurements are in papers and case series, not a public longitudinal dataset.
Almost all records are human.
rationale: Shaft length versus skin retraction is a decisive measurement, and forensic reports already discuss it. They are scattered case literature rather than an open table, and they barely cover hairy animals other than humans. Compilation can test the human case; a comparative dataset does not exist as a single resource.

operationalization: Classify teeth as continuously growing or finite, and compare that with other bones in the same species. Teeth that stop growing, or bones other than teeth that grow through life, refute the universal; continuously growing teeth alongside bones that stop would support it where that pattern holds.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: dental descriptions, including ever-growing incisors versus finite adult teeth

obstacles: Aristotle counts teeth as bones, so the comparison inherits that classification.
Continuous-growth dentition is described species by species rather than in one matrix.
rationale: Whether teeth and other skeletal elements grow through life is recorded in comparative dental accounts. Those accounts are numerous and public but not a single downloadable trait table. Misaligned teeth, his cited evidence, measure eruption and drift as well as continuous growth, which softens the test.

operationalization: Record erupted teeth or beaks at birth for humans and other toothed vertebrates, treating rare natal teeth as his 'contrary to nature' exceptions. Humans normally toothless at birth, and other toothed animals born with teeth, would support the claim; a toothed mammal or other vertebrate born toothless would refute the universal about 'other animals'.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: neonatal descriptions, including whether young are born with erupted teeth

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: altricial versus precocial life histories that correlate with natal dentition

obstacles: Natal dentition is in narrative accounts more than in a numeric column.
His 'other animals' is wider than the mammals with good birth records.
rationale: Presence or absence of teeth at birth is a yes-no trait with a clear exception class for rare natal teeth in humans. Species accounts document it for many mammals and some other vertebrates. Coverage outside familiar mammals is patchy, so the universal over all other toothed animals is only partly covered.

operationalization: Rank humans against other animals on hair cover and on nail or claw length relative to body size. Humans at the extreme of least cover and smallest nails would support the descriptive claim. 'Least earthy residue' has no separate measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass as the denominator for relative nail size where nail lengths are compiled

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian body masses for allometric comparison

obstacles: Hair cover can mean follicle density, hair length or visible nakedness, and those rankings differ.
Nail and claw lengths are not a standard column beside body mass.
rationale: Body size is tabulated, but the two traits that would decide the superlatives, hair cover and relative nail size, are scattered anatomical notes. The earthy-residue explanation is not an additional variable. A partial ranking among mammals is possible after compilation; a ranking against all animals is not.

operationalization: Count umbilical blood vessels per species and regress the count on maternal or neonatal body size. A positive size relationship matching his one-, two- and many-vessel grades would support the claim; no size trend, or vessel counts that contradict the grades, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Placentation
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of umbilical cord structure in mammals

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: adult and neonate body masses as the size axis

obstacles: Vessel counts are written in placentation accounts, not a comparative numeric file.
Humans, with three vessels at moderate size, may cut across a simple size series.
rationale: Vessel number and body size are both measurable, and placentation accounts plus mass tables supply them for a set of familiar mammals. The accounts have to be coded by hand. That is enough for a partial test of the size series, not a finished analysis of every viviparous species.

operationalization: Code viviparous mammals for upper incisors, horns and placental type, then test whether lack of upper front teeth, or a highly vascular uterus, predicts cotyledons. Cotyledons restricted to the groups he names would support the claim; cotyledons in incisor-bearing hornless species, or their absence in upper-incisor-less species, would refute the rules.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Placentation
candidate_datasets.role: placental type, including cotyledonary placentas, across mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: dental formulae, horns and reproductive accounts

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: species list and life-history context for joining dental and placental records

obstacles: Uterine vessel pattern, his second criterion, is less consistently recorded than placental type.
Camelids and a few other lineages are likely boundary cases for the incisor rule.
rationale: Placental type and the presence of upper incisors are recorded for many ungulates and other mammals in public accounts. Joining them tests the main cotyledon rule. The vessel-pattern clause and incomplete species coverage keep the full statement at a partial test rather than a single query.

operationalization: Measure placentome or cotyledon size across gestation in ruminants and test whether they shrink and vanish by term. Shrinkage to disappearance would support the claim; growth toward term, with separation only at birth, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Placentation
candidate_datasets.role: descriptions of ruminant placentomes through pregnancy

obstacles: Quantitative size-by-gestational-age series are in veterinary papers, not a shared file.
Cotyledon, caruncle and placentome are easy to conflate when coding his term.
rationale: Placentome size through pregnancy is measured in cattle and sheep and described in comparative placentation accounts. A cross-species numeric series is not downloadable as one table. The direction of size change is decidable for the main domestic ruminants after a literature compilation.

operationalization: For interspecific hybrids, record whether either sex produces offspring, and compare mules with other named crosses. Mules uniquely sterile, and every other hybrid fertile in both sexes, would support the claim; any other sterile hybrid, or a fertile mule, would refute the stated uniqueness.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of horse, ass and mule fertility

obstacles: Hybrid fertility is a literature compilation, not a global hybrid database.
Rare fertile female mules make an absolute 'sterile' claim depend on sample size.
rationale: Fertility of mules and of other hybrids is a recorded biological outcome. Public species accounts cover the equid case, while bird, canid and ray hybrids are scattered. The uniqueness claim is decidable in principle from those records and is not yet a single open analysis.

operationalization: No dataset distinguishes empty general theories from sound ones, because the claim is a rule of method rather than a statement about animals.
obstacles: The claim prescribes how natural science should argue.
It names no organism, trait or measurable outcome.
rationale: The sentence is a methodological maxim about reasoning from the principles proper to a subject. Nothing in existing biological datasets confirms or refutes it. It has no empirical decision criterion.

operationalization: Map occurrence of Equus asinus against climate, separating feral and wild records from sheltered domestic stock, and test whether breeding populations are absent from cold regions such as northern Eurasia. Absence from cold climates would support the distributional clause; established outdoor populations in cold regions would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: georeferenced observations of donkeys, including records from cold countries

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: range of the African wild ass, the wild relative of the domestic ass

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: life-history context for Equus asinus

obstacles: Domestic donkeys are moved and sheltered by people, so occurrence is not cold tolerance.
'Cold nature' is his explanation and is not the same variable as geographic range.
rationale: Occurrence data can show where asses live, including regions Aristotle called wintry. Human husbandry confounds a physiological reading of 'cannot bear cold'. The distributional clause is testable now; the innate-cold explanation is only partly constrained by those maps.

operationalization: Compare tabulated gestation lengths of horse and ass with a pre-set window around 365 days. Means and ranges inside that window for both species support a one-year gestation; a mean well outside it for either species refutes the claim for that species.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for horse and ass

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammalian gestation length at species level

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: independent compilation of gestation for the two equids

obstacles: 'One year' needs an explicit tolerance in days before the test is run.
Breed and domestication shift gestation by days to weeks.
rationale: Gestation length for both equids is a standard field in more than one open life-history database, with coverage that matches the named species. The decision is a comparison with one year and can be run directly. Only the width of the window around 365 days has to be fixed in advance.

operationalization: Measure the temperature of horse and ass semen and test whether mixing or chilling horse semen produces the sterility seen in mules. Colder ass semen, and sterility caused by that chilling, would support the mechanism; equal temperatures, or sterility unaffected by temperature, would refute it.
obstacles: No public dataset records seminal temperature of horse and ass or a chilling experiment on mule sterility.
Existing karyotype records do not measure the cold-seed mechanism.
rationale: The mechanism is a thermal prediction about the two secretions and about the effect of mixing them. That prediction is measurable, and the measurements are not in an open dataset. Sterility itself is well known, but it does not supply the temperature variable the explanation requires.

operationalization: Compile mule pregnancies and their outcomes, and record whether female mules show a menstrual or analogous uterine secretion. Conceptions that never reach birth would support the claim; a live foal would refute impossibility of birth, and an estrous rather than menstrual cycle would refute the secretion clause as he states it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mule reproductive biology, including sterility of the sexes

obstacles: Documented mule pregnancies are rare case reports.
Equids cycle by estrus, so 'menstrual secretion' is a mismatched variable.
rationale: Pregnancy outcome in female mules is an observable event, and veterinary cases plus species accounts record it. The cases are too few and too scattered for a clean rate estimate. The menstrual-secretion explanation uses a category that horse and ass reproductive physiology does not share with humans, which limits that clause.

operationalization: Code sharks, rays and chimaeras for egg-laying versus live birth and, where recorded, for shell type and egg colour. A class-wide pattern of internal eggs, live birth and a soft one-coloured egg would support the claim; oviparous species with horny egg cases would refute it as a statement about cartilaginous fishes generally.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode across sharks, rays and chimaeras

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species-level reproductive mode for chondrichthyans

obstacles: Shell hardness and egg colour are less often a separate field than reproductive mode.
Chimaeras sit at the edge of his selachian class.
rationale: Reproductive mode of cartilaginous fishes is tabulated in open trait databases with broad species coverage. Egg-laying skates and sharks are the direct counterexamples to a class-wide live-bearing claim, and they are coded. Shell colour is spottier, but the main generalization can be confirmed or refuted by a standard cross-tabulation.

operationalization: Score bird species for unfertilized eggs laid without mating, and compare ground-living prolific birds with raptors. Wind-eggs restricted to the former group would support the claim; unfertilized eggs in birds of prey, or their absence in prolific fowl, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size as a proxy for the prolific birds he contrasts with raptors

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: diet and foraging stratum to separate raptors from non-predatory birds

obstacles: Unfertilized-egg records themselves are concentrated in poultry science.
Diet and clutch size proxy the groups he names and do not record wind-eggs.
rationale: Open trait tables can separate raptors from prolific ground birds by diet and clutch size. Whether those groups lay unfertilized eggs is a further fact, well documented for fowl and geese and sparse for wild raptors. The group contrast is testable now; the wind-egg distribution is only partly compiled.

operationalization: Relate wing or feather investment to clutch size and copulation frequency, comparing raptors with heavy ground birds. A trade-off in the predicted direction would match the pattern. Shared 'residual matter' making both wings and semen is not measured by that correlation.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: wing and body measurements for birds as a proxy for allocation to flight

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size for the fecundity side of the contrast

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: diet classes that pick out birds of prey

obstacles: A correlation of wing metrics with clutch size does not show a common residual substance.
Copulation frequency is rarely tabulated beside morphology.
rationale: Wing measurements, diet and clutch size are in open bird datasets and can test whether raptors lay fewer eggs. That is the observable pattern. The material-cause story that wings and semen draw on one residue is not separated from ordinary life-history trade-offs by those variables.

operationalization: Record clutch size and nest use of Cuculus canorus against other birds. A small clutch laid in other species' nests would support the natural-history clauses. 'Cold nature' and cowardice are supported only if an independent thermal or behavioural measure predicts parasitism.

candidate_datasets.name: BirdLife Data Zone
candidate_datasets.role: species account for the common cuckoo, including brood parasitism

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size of the cuckoo relative to other birds

obstacles: Cold temperament and cowardice are not variables in ornithological trait tables.
Host-mobbing is a consequence of parasitism, so it does not independently prove a cold nature.
rationale: Brood parasitism and a small clutch are documented for the common cuckoo in public species data. Those clauses can be checked directly. The explanation from coldness and cowardice has no separate measurement in the same sources, so the claim as a whole is only partly resolvable.

operationalization: Using known-age lionesses, record litter size at each successive birth and test for the sequence from five or six down by one each year to zero. That sequence would support the claim; a different age pattern, or continued litters late in life, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: species-level litter size for the lion, a population mean rather than an age series

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: lion longevity and litter size as context for the age trajectory

obstacles: Open databases report a typical litter size, not litter size by the mother's parity.
Longitudinal lion studies exist as papers and monitoring records that still need compilation.
rationale: The predicted parity-by-parity decline is a precise, refutable series. Mean litter size in life-history databases speaks only roughly to the first-birth number. Age-specific lion reproduction is in field and zoo records that are public but scattered, so the exact sequence is partly, not immediately, testable.

operationalization: Compare egg laying in hens and geese that have never mated with birds that have mated, and score eggs as unfertilized. Eggs from never-mated females support independent origin of wind-eggs; eggs only after a prior mating would support the relic theory he rejects.
obstacles: Poultry trials are in agricultural papers and husbandry records, not one open repository.
Wild birds are outside the domestic fowl and goose evidence.
rationale: Whether a never-mated hen or goose lays eggs is a simple contrast, and poultry practice has recorded it many times. Those records are not collected as a downloadable dataset. For the domestic species he names, compilation is enough to decide the claim; it is not a ready-made analysis.

operationalization: Compare egg completeness at laying, egg size at laying versus hatching, and fecundity between birds and externally spawning fishes. Complete avian eggs and fish eggs that finish outside, with fish fecundity too high for internal completion, would support the claim; fishes that lay few complete eggs, or birds that lay unfinished ones, would challenge it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity and egg size for externally spawning fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: avian clutch size and egg mass for the bird side of the contrast

obstacles: 'Incomplete' mixes swelling, fertilization and embryonic stage.
High fecundity does not by itself show that internal completion is impossible.
rationale: Fecundity and egg size are tabulated for many fishes, and clutch and egg size for birds. That supports a comparison of numbers and of how finished the egg is at laying. The causal claim that sheer number makes internal completion impossible is not settled by the correlation alone.

operationalization: Score eggs for a distinct albumen and yolk versus a single coloured yolk mass, across birds and fishes. Two-coloured bird eggs and one-coloured fish eggs would support the claim; a bird egg without that division, or a fish egg with a separate white, would refute the corresponding universal.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: egg descriptions and diameters for fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: bird egg sizes as context; yolk-and-white structure is only partly captured

obstacles: Yolk-versus-white structure is described in embryology texts more than in a trait column.
Shark eggs are structurally richer than typical teleost eggs.
rationale: The colour division of the egg is a visible trait with a clear contrast between birds and fishes. Fish and bird databases record egg size much more consistently than albumen-yolk structure. The contrast can be checked from existing descriptions for many species and is not a finished comparative file.

operationalization: Compare yolk mass and yolk colour between water birds and land birds, holding egg size constant. Larger and paler yolks in water birds would support the descriptive claim; equal or smaller, deeper-yellow yolks would refute it. Moister and colder nature is a separate proxy.

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: foraging and habitat classes that separate aquatic from terrestrial birds

obstacles: Yolk proportion and yolk colour are in poultry and ornithology papers, not in the habitat tables.
Domestication and diet change yolk colour independently of habitat.
rationale: Habitat classifications can pick out water birds and land birds. Yolk size and colour, the traits that decide the claim, are measured for some domestic and wild species in scattered studies. The group labels are ready; the yolk comparison still has to be compiled, and diet confounds colour.

operationalization: Record which end of the egg emerges first at oviposition in domestic fowl and other birds. The blunt end first, sharp end last, would support the claim; sharp end first in a majority of layings would refute it.
obstacles: Orientation at laying is in poultry observations and films, not a public dataset.
Other bird species are much less often recorded than the hen.
rationale: Which pole emerges first is a binary observation with a decisive count. Poultry research has recorded it for the domestic fowl, in scattered reports rather than an open table. Extending the same count to birds generally would need further compiled observations.

operationalization: Measure shell hardness and mineral content at the moment of laying and over the following minutes, and test whether hardening is produced by cooling and evaporation. A soft shell at exit that rigidifies by cooling would support the claim; a shell already hard in the shell gland, with no post-laying mineral jump, would refute it.
obstacles: Shell-gland timing is in poultry physiology papers, not a shared dataset.
Cooling and evaporation need to be separated from calcification that happened before laying.
rationale: Hardness at laying versus hardness after a short interval is a direct test, and poultry physiology has measured calcification in the shell gland. Those measurements are scattered and mostly about the domestic fowl. They are sufficient to assess the hen and only a start for birds generally.

operationalization: For live-bearing selachians, especially smooth-hounds, record whether the embryo remains attached to the uterus by a cord after the yolk is exhausted. Attachment by an umbilicus at that stage confirms the claim; yolk-only nutrition with no cord, in the species he indicates, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode, including placental viviparity, for Mustelus and relatives

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of smooth-hound reproduction

obstacles: Reproductive-mode categories do not time the cord against yolk exhaustion.
Anatomical descriptions of the umbilicus are fuller in papers than in the trait tables.
rationale: Placental viviparity of smooth-hounds is coded in elasmobranch trait databases and identifies the maternal connection. The further detail that a cord persists after the yolk is used sits in anatomical accounts that still need reading. The species-level fact is close to a direct query; the timing clause is a partial extra.

operationalization: Estimate the fraction of eggs that die before hatch for oviparous fishes and compare it with fecundity. Most eggs destroyed, and higher fecundity where early mortality is higher, would support the numerical pattern. 'Nature makes up for the destruction' is not a separate result.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity and early-life traits for marine and freshwater fishes

candidate_datasets.name: RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database
candidate_datasets.role: stock-recruitment series that constrain egg and early-life survival for assessed fishes

obstacles: Egg mortality is well estimated mainly for commercial species.
A fecundity-mortality correlation does not test a purposive compensation by nature.
rationale: Fecundity tables and stock-recruitment series can show that early survival is low in many fishes and that egg number is high. Coverage is biased to fisheries species. The teleological clause that nature compensates by numbers does not add a measurement beyond that pattern.

operationalization: Tabulate fishes by sexual system and count hermaphroditic or unisexual species besides the candidates for erythrinus and channa. Separate sexes in all but those two kinds would support the claim; additional hermaphrodites or all-female species would refute the exception list.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: hermaphroditism and sex records across fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex
candidate_datasets.role: sexual systems for hundreds of fish species

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: names for matching erythrinus and channa to modern genera

obstacles: The two named exceptions are probable serranids, not certain species identifications.
rationale: Sexual system is a coded field for a large fraction of fishes, including many hermaphrodites beyond any two Mediterranean names. That is enough to confirm or refute the claim that separate sexes fail in only two kinds. Uncertainty about those two names affects the exception list, not the existence of further exceptions.

operationalization: Trace the path from the mouth in fishes and record whether it opens into the gut or the gonad, and code fertilization as external, internal or oral. A gut-bound oral path, with fertilization elsewhere, refutes conception by swallowing milt; a demonstrated route from swallowed milt to the ovary would support that theory.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fertilization mode and reproductive guild, including mouth-brooding as distinct from conception

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish anatomical ontology of the digestive tract versus the gonads

obstacles: Mouth-brooding can be misread as oral conception unless the fertilization stage is coded separately.
rationale: Fertilization mode is tabulated for many fishes, and anatomical resources separate the digestive tract from the reproductive tract. Together they test the swallowing theory directly: oral incubation, where it occurs, is not a path into the ovary. The distinction is standard and does not need new dissection.

operationalization: Dissection records and anatomical descriptions score whether hyenas are hermaphrodites or have one sexual apparatus per individual, and whether both sexes bear a female-like mark under the tail. One sex organ per animal, plus a shared subcaudal mark, would support the claim; functional male and female organs in one individual would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: spotted hyena anatomy, including the female pseudopenis

obstacles: The spotted hyena's pseudopenis is easy to mis-score as a second sex.
Striped and brown hyenas differ and may not be the animal he saw.
rationale: Hyena genital anatomy is described in public species accounts and in a large anatomical literature, enough to test hermaphroditism versus a single apparatus. The accounts are narrative rather than a specimen-level dataset. Which hyena species he meant changes the fit of the 'line under the tail'.

operationalization: In hens mated first to one cock and then to another, genotype the embryos of eggs fertilized before the second mating. A switch of those embryos to the second sire would support telegony; embryos that match the first sire, with the second sire appearing only in later eggs, would refute change of an already fertilized egg.
obstacles: Parentage trials are in older poultry papers and modern sperm-competition studies, not one archive.
Later mating can fertilize later eggs, which must not be scored as change of already fertilized eggs.
rationale: Genetic parentage of a specified egg is a decisive test of whether a later cock overwrites an earlier fertilization. Such trials exist in the poultry and sperm-competition literature and have to be compiled. The timing clause, before white separates from yolk, is rarely the exact design, so the test covers the claim in part.

operationalization: For bees, wasps and caterpillars, score whether the full-grown larva enters a quiescent, hardened stage before the adult. A motionless pupa or puparium would support the claim for those insects; direct transformation without a quiescent stage would refute it for that group.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: Drosophila life-cycle stages, including the immobile pupa, as a holometabolous model

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: photographic records of bee, wasp and lepidopteran pupae

obstacles: A trait table of pupation across Hymenoptera and Lepidoptera is not a single download.
Aristotle's 'egg' for this stage is the pupa, and the mapping should stay explicit.
rationale: The pupal stage of flies is documented in a model-organism database, and pupae of bees, wasps and moths are widely recorded. That is enough to test the named examples. A complete matrix for every scolex-producing insect is still a compilation, so the universal reading stays partial.

operationalization: Identify insects that appear in wool and in water and reconstruct whether they hatch from eggs laid after mating. Parentage and eggs would refute spontaneous origin; repeated appearance in sterile media with no eggs would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence of clothes moths and aquatic insects, without life-cycle closure by itself

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproduction and larval notes for aquatic invertebrates

obstacles: Wool insects such as clothes moths are poorly covered by marine life-history databases.
Occurrence records show where insects are found, not that they arose without parents.
rationale: Life cycles of clothes moths and of aquatic insect larvae are known from entomological accounts and, for many aquatic species, from public reproduction notes. Those notes refute parentless origin where eggs and mating are recorded. The records are uneven for the wool-dwelling cases, so the existential claim is only partly covered by ready datasets.

operationalization: In honey-bee colonies, determine who lays drone eggs and whether those eggs are unfertilized. Drones from unfertilized worker-laid eggs would support the claim; drones only from the queen, or drones from fertilized eggs, would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Hymenoptera Genome Database
candidate_datasets.role: Apis mellifera genome resources, including the sex-determination locus behind haploid drones

obstacles: Genome resources show how haploid eggs become drones, not which caste lays them.
Laying-worker observations are in beekeeping studies rather than a public colony table.
rationale: Haplodiploid sex determination is documented in honey-bee genomic resources and predicts drones from unfertilized eggs. Who lays those eggs, workers or the queen, is a colony-level fact recorded in beekeeping research that still has to be compiled. The genetic half is ready; the caste half is partial.

operationalization: Track maternity in honey-bee hives: whether the queen (his 'king') is the mother of new queens and of workers. Queen maternity of both castes would support the claim; workers or drones producing either caste would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Hymenoptera Genome Database
candidate_datasets.role: honey-bee genetic resources used in parentage and sex-determination studies

obstacles: Caste is nutritional as well as genetic, so 'generate workers' is not just fertilization.
Colony pedigrees are in apicultural papers more than in the genome browser.
rationale: Queen-right colonies and genetic markers can assign maternity of workers and of new queens, and honey-bee genetic resources support that kind of study. The primary observations are breeding records rather than a single open pedigree file. The claim is testable for Apis mellifera with moderate extra compilation.

operationalization: Pair colony censuses of drones and workers with local weather, and test whether fair seasons yield more drones and rainy seasons more workers, holding forage constant. That seasonal split would support the claim; no weather association, or the reverse, would refute it.
obstacles: Public hive-monitoring series rarely publish drone and worker counts against weather.
Season, forage and rainfall are collinear, so a rain effect is hard to isolate.
rationale: Drone and worker numbers versus weather are countable, and beekeepers have long noted seasonal drone production. An open matched dataset of caste counts and rainfall is not in hand. Existing notes can support a partial test and leave the rain-versus-fair contrast weakly controlled.

operationalization: No measurement confirms or refutes a rule that observation should outrank theory, because the sentence is a norm for inquiry.
obstacles: The claim is methodological.
Agreement of a theory with facts is a standard of judgment, not a biological variable.
rationale: Aristotle is stating how credit should be assigned between observations and theories. Datasets of animal traits do not decide that norm. The claim has no empirical scope to resolve.

operationalization: Count shelled molluscs flagged as marine versus terrestrial, treating land snails as his stated exception. A small terrestrial fauna beside a large marine one would support 'few on land'; a terrestrial species richness of the same order as the marine fauna would refute 'few'.

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: environment flags (marine, freshwater, terrestrial) for molluscs

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic catalogue of molluscs, including terrestrial gastropods

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence records of land snails and marine shells as a geographic check

obstacles: 'Few' needs a pre-set fraction of species or of higher taxa.
His testaceans sometimes include barnacles and other non-molluscs.
rationale: Environment is a coded attribute in the standard mollusc registers, so marine and terrestrial species can be counted directly. Land snails are in those registers, which is the comparison he invites. Once a threshold for 'few' is fixed, the count confirms or refutes the biogeographic claim with ordinary queries.

operationalization: Count molluscs, cephalopods and crustaceans in fresh water, brackish water and the sea, using environment flags and occurrence salinity. Near-absence from lakes, with concentration in estuaries, would support the claim; diverse freshwater faunas would refute 'only exceptionally'.

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: marine, brackish and freshwater flags for molluscs and crustaceans

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: marine and coastal occurrence records, including estuaries

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: freshwater and marine mollusc catalogues

obstacles: 'Bloodless' bundles molluscs, cephalopods and crustaceans, which differ in freshwater tolerance.
'Exceptionally' needs a numeric cutoff.
rationale: Habitat and salinity are coded well enough to compare lakes, estuaries and the sea for these groups. Freshwater mussels, snails and crayfishes are in the same registers as marine species. A standard count can confirm or refute a claim of near-absence from fresh water.

operationalization: Reconstruct the life cycle of Anguilla and of candidate river mullets from spawning location, larvae and parentage. Eggs, larvae and migrating adults would refute origin without parents from earth-entrails; animals arising in mud with no gametes or larvae would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: life cycle, spawning and distribution of freshwater eels

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: marine occurrence of eel larvae and spawning-area records

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: names linking river eels to Anguilla and its leptocephalus stages

obstacles: The mullet of the claim is unidentified.
'Entrails of earth' may be worms or mud rather than a biological stage, which complicates the larval identification.
rationale: The eel life cycle, including marine spawning and a larval stage, is documented in open biogeographic and fisheries databases. That record decides the parentless-origin claim for the eel, which is the central case. The unnamed mullet and the identity of the earth-entrails are side uncertainties, not a bar to testing the eel.

operationalization: Code testaceans for sexual reproduction, eggs or larvae versus appearance from mud with no parents. Documented eggs, veligers or other larvae refute universal spontaneous generation; a species with no gametes or larvae whose recruits appear only from putrefying mud would support the claim for that species.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproduction and larval development of marine molluscs and other invertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic scope of shelled molluscs to which the universal applies

candidate_datasets.name: WoRMS
candidate_datasets.role: species list and environment for bivalves, gastropods and barnacles

obstacles: Larval mode is filled for commercial and well-studied species more than for the whole fauna.
Aristotle's testaceans include animals that are not molluscs.
rationale: Reproduction and larval type are recorded for many bivalves, gastropods and barnacles in open marine databases. Any such sexual life cycle refutes a universal claim of spontaneous generation from mud. Coverage is incomplete, but it is already wide enough for a standard query to decide the universal.

operationalization: In twin and multiparous pregnancies of mammals and live-bearing fishes, record the sex of embryos that share a uterine horn or chamber. Frequent mixed-sex pairs in the same region would support the claim; sexes consistently segregated by uterine region would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Placentation
candidate_datasets.role: uterine and fetal arrangement in mammals, sometimes noting twins

obstacles: Sex-by-uterine-position is rarely a coded field.
Live-bearing fishes and land mammals need different anatomical maps of 'the same part'.
rationale: Veterinary and clinical records can locate twin sexes within the uterus, and placentation accounts describe uterine layout. A dataset built for this contrast does not exist. Mixed-sex sharing can be checked for a few well-studied species and not for viviparous animals at large.

operationalization: Score male fishes and snakes for the presence of testes, and separately record how sex is determined. Absence of testes together with both sexes would support his anatomical premise; testes in both groups would refute that premise. Whether testes 'determine' sex is then read from sex-determination records.

candidate_datasets.name: ZFIN
candidate_datasets.role: zebrafish gonadal anatomy, including testes

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: maturity and sex records showing male and female fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex
candidate_datasets.role: sex-determination systems of fishes and reptiles

obstacles: Aristotle reserved 'testes' for compact mammalian organs and did not count elongated fish and snake gonads.
Sex-determination mechanism is a different variable from presence of the organ.
rationale: Anatomical databases and fish records document male gonads in fishes, and reptile and fish sex systems are tabulated. That tests the claim that these animals lack testes and still produce both sexes. His narrower meaning of 'testes' has to be translated into modern gonad terms before the anatomical clause is settled.

operationalization: No assay separates 'concocting blood into semen that carries the principle of form' from the definition of the male, because form-bearing concoction is not a measured variable.
obstacles: The sentence defines the male rather than predicting a trait.
'Principle of form' is a metaphysical role for semen.
rationale: Aristotle is defining the sexes by a capacity to concoct formative semen. Semen can be chemically described, but that description does not capture 'principle of form' or decide the definition. The claim is conceptual.

operationalization: Compare sex-specific body temperature or resting metabolic rate within species. Males hotter across species would support a thermal reading; females hotter, or no consistent sex difference, would refute that reading of the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: species-level body temperature, rarely split by sex

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: metabolic parameters that can be compared between sexes only where studies report both

obstacles: Innate heat is inferred from his theory of concoction, not defined as core temperature.
Most thermal tables are species means, not paired sex measurements.
rationale: A within-species sex difference in temperature or metabolism is measurable, and some data exist. Open compilations usually collapse the sexes, so the comparison has to be rebuilt from papers. Even a clear temperature result only proxies the innate heat the argument is about.

operationalization: Compare sex-determination mechanisms with a heat-failure rule that females result when the male principle is too cool to master the material. A general association of lower developmental temperature with female offspring would support that rule; genetic sex determination, or lineages in which heat produces males, would refute it as a universal mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Tree of Sex
candidate_datasets.role: sex-determination mode, including chromosomal systems and temperature-dependent sex determination

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: reptile species for which temperature-dependent sex determination is reported

obstacles: Temperature-dependent sex determination does not have one direction across reptiles.
Mammalian and avian chromosomal sex is not a failure of heat.
rationale: Sex-determination mode is tabulated widely enough to confront a single heat-failure mechanism. The tables show multiple mechanisms, which can refute universality, and they do not measure his 'mastery' of material. The claim is testable as a general rule and not as a quantified thermal threshold.

operationalization: Regress offspring sex on parental age, comparing young and old parents with parents in their prime. A higher female fraction at both age extremes would support the claim; a flat or opposite pattern would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific human fertility schedules, a frame for parental age but not offspring sex by itself

obstacles: Age-specific sex ratios sit in civil-registration microdata that are often restricted or scattered.
Animal breeding records are uneven outside a few domestic species.
rationale: Offspring sex by parental age is a standard demographic contrast, and human fertility schedules fix the age axis. The sex-of-birth tables needed for the test are public in some countries and closed or dispersed in others. Humans can be examined in part; the animal universal still needs compilation.

operationalization: Link estimated conception dates to prevailing wind direction and compare the sex ratio of births conceived under northerly versus southerly winds. A higher male fraction under north winds would support the claim; no difference would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Copernicus Climate Data Store
candidate_datasets.role: reanalysis winds that could be joined to conception dates if birth microdata are available

obstacles: Conception date is inferred from birth date and is noisy.
Public birth records with usable dates and open wind series are not already joined, and many microdata extracts are restricted.
rationale: Wind at conception and sex at birth are both recorded kinds of data, and gridded winds are openly available. A linked public analysis file is not. Building the link is a real harmonization task with weak power once conception timing error is admitted, so the claim is only marginally testable now.

operationalization: Test the distribution of menstrual onset across lunar phase, with the waning half as the predicted mode. An excess in the waning moon would support the claim; a uniform or waxing-moon excess would refute it.
obstacles: Onset dates aligned to the lunar calendar are in separate clinical studies.
Cycle length near 29 days can create an apparent lunar match that has to be modelled explicitly.
rationale: Lunar phase at menstrual onset is a well-defined circular statistic, and published cycle diaries bear on it. There is no single open multi-cohort table. A compilation can test the timing claim; it is not a dataset one can download and run immediately.

operationalization: Compute phenotypic similarity against kinship, comparing parent-offspring, grandparent-grandchild and unrelated pairs. Similarity declining in that order would support the claim; a flat or reversed gradient would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal QTLdb
candidate_datasets.role: pedigree-based trait loci in livestock, evidence of parent-offspring transmission rather than a kinship-gradient table

obstacles: The clean kinship gradient lives in restricted or study-specific pedigrees.
QTL catalogues show that traits are heritable and do not report grandparent correlations directly.
rationale: Resemblance by degree of relatedness is a standard quantitative-genetic measurement, and animal breeding pedigrees contain it. Open QTL compilations document heritability without tabulating the parent-versus-ancestor contrast. The claim is decidable from existing pedigrees after access and compilation, not from one fully open file.

operationalization: In pedigrees where a child misses the father's traits, test whether resemblance moves next to the grandfather and then the great-grandfather, and likewise on the mother's side. That ordered reversion would support the claim; resemblance jumping without that order would refute the sequence of 'resolved movements'.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal QTLdb
candidate_datasets.role: cross and pedigree trait data in which ancestral resemblance can be studied only indirectly

obstacles: Segregation and recombination produce grandparent resemblance without a semen-movement cascade.
The mechanism names movements in the semen, which pedigrees do not record.
rationale: An ordered fallback from father to grandfather to earlier ancestors is a pedigree pattern that can be counted. Public genetic resources show hereditary transmission and do not record seminal movements or that specific order. The pattern is only a weak proxy for the mechanism, and most outcomes fit genetic inheritance as well.

operationalization: Compare rates of congenital malformation per offspring, and per birth, across species binned by litter or clutch size, with domestic fowl singled out. Rates rising from uniparous animals to multiparous mammals to fowl would support the claim; equal per-offspring rates, or a peak elsewhere, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: litter and clutch size, the fecundity axis of the comparison

candidate_datasets.name: DevTox
candidate_datasets.role: developmental-anomaly records for laboratory vertebrates, biased toward toxicant assays

obstacles: Natural malformation rates are confounded with how closely embryos are inspected, especially in poultry.
Toxicology anomaly databases are not surveys of wild or farm monstrosities.
rationale: Litter and clutch size are tabulated, so the groups he ranks can be defined. Rates of spontaneous monstrosity are not in the same tables and are inflated where many eggs are opened. A partial, bias-aware comparison is possible; a clean ranking across animals is not.
